name: Beth Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for meeting me, Beth. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union or party, and what you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage the mortgage processing team at one of the big bank's back-office centres, ten people. We check the applications after the advisers have sold them: payslips, valuations, ID, all of it, then we send the offer out. I'm at my desk by eight, I go through the overnight queue and decide who takes what.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that a family gets the keys because we did it properly. What wears me out is the systems, honestly, they change something every few months and I'm the one who has to explain it. I don't touch the AI chat things, I prefer to read the documents myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, because a lot of it was always salesmanship. At church on Sunday I'd say it to the older ladies who worry about it. I don't post online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd still have things on my mind. Tomas and I are getting married next June, and the wedding is eating our savings. And the bank has closed two processing centres in the last four years, so mine isn't guaranteed either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job well, which is the best protection there is. We'd cut the wedding guest list from a hundred and twenty to eighty and keep about four months of savings back. I wouldn't change anything at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. Not about AI, about money and the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when those two centres closed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They moved the work up north to a bigger centre, where it's cheaper. Some people moved, most didn't. I couldn't move, Tomas's work is here and so is my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Tomas feel about cutting the guest list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas wants a big wedding, his family is big. But I've grown up being careful with money, and I'd rather start married life without debt, even if the wedding is smaller. We'd find a way.

say: I'm **not surprised**; a lot of AI was always salesmanship.
I'd say it at **church** to the older ladies, not online.
think: The **wedding** next June is eating our savings.
The bank closed **two processing centres**, so mine isn't guaranteed.
do: Keep doing the **job well** as the best protection.
Cut the **guest list** from a hundred and twenty to eighty.
Keep about **four months** of savings back.
feel: **Uneasy**, about money and the bank rather than AI.
S0.quote: I'd rather start married life without debt, even if the wedding is smaller.
fieldNote: Her unease is about **wedding costs** and centre closures, not AI.
**Rooted** locally: won't move away from her mum and Tomas's work.
Values **thrift** and doing the job properly.

steps.text: Cut the wedding guest list from 120 to 80
Keep processing mortgages exactly as now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses will do what they think is right, and it's their business. At work I'd say we should be careful, because a wrong mortgage offer ruins a family. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, checking payslips and documents is exactly the sort of thing the bank will give to a computer. I think my ten becomes five, maybe fewer. And they'd merge the teams and keep one manager, and I'm not sure it'd be me, because I don't use the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever they put in front of me, because I'd have to, but I wouldn't go looking. I'd save harder, push the wedding to a registry office and a meal, and keep the money. I'd ask my pastor if he knows anyone at the council or the schools who's hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like being told there's a review and you don't know the date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said businesses should do what they think is right. Should the bank use AI, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I suppose they should, yes. But I'd want it slower. It's the speed I don't trust, and the people selling it to the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible, if your team shrank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The salesmen, mostly. The consultants and tech firms who tell the bank it'll save millions. Not the bank, really, they have to compete.

say: Businesses do what they think right; **it's their business**.
Be careful, because a **wrong mortgage offer** ruins a family.
think: **Checking documents** is exactly what goes to a computer.
Ten could become **five**, and the remaining manager may not be me.
do: Learn the new tools **only if required**.
Switch to a **registry office** wedding and a meal.
Ask my **pastor** about council or school jobs.
S1.quote: Checking payslips and documents is exactly the sort of thing the bank will give to a computer.
fieldNote: Sees her own **role at risk** because she avoids the new tools.
Free-market view: blames **consultants** and sellers, not the bank.
Turns to **church** networks for job leads.

steps.text: Change to a registry office wedding and a family meal
Put the saved wedding money into savings
Ask the pastor about council and school job openings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has gone too far and too fast, and I'd say it without shouting. At church I'd say we need to look after each other. Online, still nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job is gone in the first year. All of it is reading and checking, and the whole back office goes, in every bank. My fiancé Tomas is an electrician, so he's got three more years before the robots, and that's the only thing that keeps me steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd postpone the wedding by a year, or just do the registry office with family. I'd apply to be a teaching assistant at the church primary, because that's people work. And Tomas and I would live on his wage and save all of mine while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I wouldn't sleep well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want government support in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some, but I'd rather work than take it. Family first, then the church, then the council. That's how I was brought up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when the robots come for Tomas's work in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what keeps me up at night. Three years is something. After that, I just don't know, and I'd pray about it.

say: This has gone too far and **too fast**.
At church I'd say we need to **look after each other**.
think: My job is **gone** in the first year, with every bank back office.
Tomas has **three more years** as an electrician before robots.
do: **Postpone** the wedding or do a registry office with family.
Apply as a **teaching assistant** at the church primary.
Live on **Tomas's wage** and save all of mine.
S2.quote: My fiancé Tomas is an electrician, so he's got three more years before the robots, and that's the only thing that keeps me steady.
fieldNote: Expects to **lose her job** within a year.
The household leans on **Tomas's hands-on** job and its three-year gap.
Prefers **family and church** to government help.

steps.text: Postpone the wedding a year or do a registry office
Apply as a teaching assistant at the church primary school
Live on Tomas's wage and bank her own pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this sensibly, if people keep their heads. At work I'd ask the managers what the plan is. I'd say it at church too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job goes by 2031, like the fast one, just later. Five years is enough to get a qualification in something with people. I'd be thirty-two and hopefully a mum by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the bank and keep my head down for two or three years. I'd do a teaching assistant course in the evenings from the second year. We'd still get married next June, smaller, and save hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but less sharp. More of a dread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned being a mum. Would this change your plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, we'd still want them. But maybe a year or two later, until I know what my job is. My fiancé Tomas would say God provides, and I'd say God provides a savings account too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not learn the AI tools with five years to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd rather put my effort into a job that needs a person in the room. I know it's stubborn. But I'm not good with that stuff, and I'd be competing with people who are.

say: There's **time** to do this sensibly if people keep their heads.
I'd ask the managers at the bank for **the plan**.
think: My job **goes by 2031**, just later than the fast picture.
Five years is enough for a **qualification** in something with people.
do: Stay at the bank for **two or three years**.
Take an evening **teaching assistant** course from year two.
Marry next June, **smaller**, and save hard.
feel: **Alarmed** but less sharp, more of a **dread**.
S3.quote: My fiancé Tomas would say God provides, and I'd say God provides a savings account too.
fieldNote: Still expects to **lose the bank job**; time changes the route, not the end.
Children **delayed** a year or two until her work is clear.

steps.text: Start an evening teaching assistant course in year two
Hold a smaller wedding next June and save the difference
Delay trying for children by a year or two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and things never go the way people predict. At work I'd say let's not panic. At church I'd say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd have most of the decade in the bank. I'd be thirty-seven in 2036, probably with children, and that's when it'd bite. I'd want to have moved before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job, and I'd wait a few years to see whether the predictions come true. I'd save steadily and get married next June as planned. If it started to happen, I'd do the teaching assistant course around year four or five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but quietly. It's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't waiting a few years a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I've seen lots of things that were coming and never came, so I'd rather be steady than jump at every headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Tomas in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas would be fine until about 2039, robots are later. And he could teach apprentices. I worry more about my mum, who works on a supermarket till.

say: Ten years is **a long time**, and predictions often fail.
Let's **not panic**, at work or at church.
think: I'd have **most of the decade** in the bank.
It would bite at **thirty-seven**, probably with young children at home.
do: Keep the job and **wait** to see if predictions come true.
Marry **next June** as planned and save steadily.
Start the **teaching assistant** course around year four if needed.
feel: **Anxious**, but quietly, because it is far off.
S4.quote: I've seen lots of things that were coming and never came, so I'd rather be steady than jump at every headline.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **resistant**, wait-and-see instinct lead.
Still expects the job to **end** when children are young.
Worries for her **mum** on a supermarket till.

steps.text: Keep the mortgage processing job and watch for changes
Put a set amount into savings each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My job goes, the wedding gets pushed back, and we're living on Tomas's wage with a clock on that too. What would help is apprenticeships and proper training for real jobs, paid by the companies, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe faith and community. People talk like it's all money and jobs. But when the processing centres closed, it was the church that fed people, not the bank.

headlineQuote: When the processing centres closed, it was the church that fed people, not the bank.
portrait: Beth, 27, manages a **ten-person** mortgage processing team at a bank and marries Tomas, an electrician, next June.
She has never used AI tools and prefers to **read documents** herself.
Traditional and pro-market, she blames **consultants** selling AI more than the bank.
She is uneasy even in AI Plateau because of **wedding costs** and past closures.
Her plan is a **teaching assistant** role and leaning on Tomas, family and church.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, when her job goes and **the wedding** is pushed back.
whatWouldHelp: Company-paid **apprenticeships** and training for real jobs, **not handouts**.
